statement: For every finite [graph](c:graph) with positive edge weights, the matching [polynomial](c:polynomial) has only real roots. Equivalently, the [partition function](c:partition-function) of the [monomer-dimer model](c:dimer-model) vanishes only at negative real activities.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is a finite simple [graph](c:graph).
Every edge weight satisfies $w_e > 0$.

conclusion: All roots of $\mu_G(x) = \sum_k (-1)^k m_k x^{n-2k}$ are real, and all zeros of $Z_G(\lambda) = \sum_k m_k \lambda^k$ are negative reals.

proofs.name: Induction with a ratio in the upper half-plane
proofs.slogan: Delete one vertex at a time and keep the ratio of matching polynomials in the upper half-plane.
proofs.scope: Every finite simple graph with positive edge weights.

roles.why: A finite graph lets the induction on the number of vertices start and stop.
Positive weights keep each correction term in the upper half-plane, so imaginary parts only grow.

steps.slogan: Split [matchings](c:matching) by what happens at one vertex.
steps.detail: Either $u$ is unmatched or it is matched to a neighbour $v$, which gives $\mu_G = x\mu_{G-u} - \sum_{v \sim u} w_{uv}\mu_{G-u-v}$, a [recurrence relation](c:recurrence-relation).

steps.slogan: Claim that the ratio of polynomials lies in the [upper half-plane](c:upper-half-plane).
steps.detail: For $\operatorname{Im} z > 0$ the claim is $\mu_G(z) \ne 0$ and $\operatorname{Im}(\mu_G(z)/\mu_{G-u}(z)) \ge \operatorname{Im} z$, which holds for a single vertex.

steps.slogan: Minus a positive multiple of an inverse upper half-plane point stays in the upper half-plane.
steps.detail: Dividing the recurrence by $\mu_{G-u}$ gives $z - \sum_v w_{uv}/g_v$ with $\operatorname{Im} g_v > 0$ by induction, and each $-w_{uv}/g_v$ has positive imaginary part.

steps.slogan: Real coefficients reflect the zero-free upper half-plane to the lower half-plane.
steps.detail: Since $\mu_G(\bar z)$ is the [complex conjugation](c:complex-conjugation) of $\mu_G(z)$, there are no non-real [roots](c:root-of-a-polynomial) at all.

steps.slogan: Substitute $\lambda = -1/x^2$ to pass to the monomer-dimer partition function.
steps.detail: Because $\mu_G(x) = x^n Z_G(-1/x^2)$, a zero of $Z_G$ off the negative axis would give a non-real root of $\mu_G$.

new_concepts.name: dimer model
new_concepts.reminder: The dimer model is a random perfect matching of a graph, such as a random domino tiling.
new_concepts.definition: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite [graph](c:graph) with edge weights $w(e)>0$. The dimer model on $G$ is the probability measure on the set of [perfect matchings](c:perfect-matching) $M$ of $G$ given by $\mathbb P(M)=Z^{-1}\prod_{e\in M}w(e)$, where $Z=\sum_M\prod_{e\in M}w(e)$. With all weights equal to $1$ it is the uniform perfect matching, and for planar $G$ Kasteleyn's theorem writes $Z$ as a Pfaffian.

statement: On a finite graph, one joint measure on spins and edges has the q-state [Potts model](c:potts-model) as spin marginal and the [random-cluster model](c:random-cluster-model) as edge marginal. This [coupling](c:coupling-of-measures) turns spin correlations into connection probabilities.

hypotheses.text: The [graph](c:graph) $G = (V, E)$ is finite.
The number of spin values $q \ge 2$ is an integer, $p \in (0,1)$, and $J = -\ln(1-p)$.

conclusion: The measure $P(\sigma,\omega) \propto \prod_{xy}[(1-p)1_{\omega_{xy}=0} + p\,1_{\omega_{xy}=1}1_{\sigma_x=\sigma_y}]$ has Potts marginal $\propto e^{J\sum 1_{\sigma_x=\sigma_y}}$ and random-cluster marginal $\propto p^{o(\omega)}(1-p)^{c(\omega)}q^{k(\omega)}$. Given $\omega$, clusters get independent uniform colours. Given $\sigma$, agreeing edges open with probability $p$. Also $\mu(\sigma_x=\sigma_y) = 1/q + (1-1/q)\,\phi(x \leftrightarrow y)$.

proofs.name: Summing the joint weight over one coordinate
proofs.slogan: The joint weight is a product over edges that vanishes on incompatible pairs, so each marginal is a simple sum.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, items (a) to (e), on every finite graph.

roles.why: Finiteness makes all sums finite and the normalizing constant positive.
An integer $q$ gives $q^{k(\omega)}$ colourings, and $1-p = e^{-J}$ turns the edge sum into the Potts weight.

steps.slogan: Write the joint weight as $p^{o}(1-p)^{c}$ on compatible pairs and zero elsewhere.
steps.detail: A pair is compatible when every open edge joins equal spins. The product of edge factors equals $p^{o(\omega)}(1-p)^{c(\omega)}$ for compatible pairs and vanishes otherwise, and the constant spin with all edges closed has positive weight.

steps.slogan: Sum over edges to get the [Potts model](c:potts-model) weight of each spin configuration.
steps.detail: For fixed $\sigma$ the sum factorizes over edges. An agreeing edge contributes $1$ and a disagreeing edge contributes $1-p = e^{-J}$, so the sum is $e^{-J|E|}\exp(J\sum 1_{\sigma_x=\sigma_y})$.

steps.slogan: Sum over spins to get the [random-cluster model](c:random-cluster-model) weight of each edge configuration.
steps.detail: For fixed $\omega$ the compatible spins are those constant on each [cluster](c:connected-component), and there are $q^{k(\omega)}$ of them. So the sum is $p^{o(\omega)}(1-p)^{c(\omega)}q^{k(\omega)}$.

steps.slogan: Read off both [conditional](c:conditional-probability) laws from the product form of the weight.
steps.detail: Given $\omega$, the weight is constant on compatible $\sigma$, so clusters receive independent [uniform](c:uniform-distribution) colours. Given $\sigma$, the weight is a product of edge factors, so disagreeing edges are closed and agreeing edges are open with probability $p$.

steps.slogan: Average the colouring rule over $\omega$ to express spin agreement through connection probabilities.
steps.detail: Given $\omega$, two connected vertices agree surely and two unconnected vertices agree with probability $1/q$. Averaging gives $\mu(\sigma_x=\sigma_y) = 1/q + (1-1/q)\phi(x \leftrightarrow y)$, which for the [Ising model](c:ising-model) reads $\langle \sigma_x\sigma_y\rangle = \phi(x \leftrightarrow y)$.

new_concepts.reminder: A coupling of $\mu$ and $\nu$ is a joint law of a pair $(X,Y)$ with $X\sim\mu$ and $Y\sim\nu$.

A coupling of [probability measures](c:probability-measure) $\mu$ on $S$ and $
u$ on $T$ is a probability measure $\gamma$ on $S	imes T$ whose [marginals](c:marginal-distribution) are $\mu$ and $
u$, that is, $\gamma(A	imes T)=\mu(A)$ and $\gamma(S	imes B)=
u(B)$. Equivalently, it is a pair of random variables $(X,Y)$ on one probability space with $X\sim\mu$ and $Y\sim
u$. When $S=T$, every coupling satisfies $\|\mu-
u\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\mathbb P(X

new_concepts.name: Bernoulli percolation
new_concepts.reminder: Bernoulli percolation keeps each edge of a graph independently with probability $p$ and studies the connected clusters.
new_concepts.definition: Bernoulli bond percolation with parameter $p\in[0,1]$ on a [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$ declares each edge open with probability $p$ and closed otherwise, independently of all other edges. Its law is the [product measure](c:product-measure) $\mathbb P_p=\bigotimes_{e\in E}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ on $\{0,1\}^E$. The open clusters are the [connected components](c:connected-component) of the graph $(V,\{e:\omega(e)=1\})$, and site percolation does the same with vertices.

new_concepts.name: Potts model
new_concepts.reminder: The Potts model gives each vertex one of $q$ states and rewards neighbors that are in the same state.
new_concepts.definition: The $q$-state Potts model on a finite [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$ is the [Gibbs distribution](c:gibbs-distribution) on $\{1,\dots,q\}^V$ given by $\mu_\beta(\sigma)=Z^{-1}\exp(\beta\sum_{xy\in E}\mathbf 1\{\sigma_x=\sigma_y\})$. Its Hamiltonian is $H(\sigma)=-\sum_{xy\in E}\mathbf 1\{\sigma_x=\sigma_y\}$, and $\beta>0$ gives the ferromagnetic model. For $q=2$ it is the [Ising model](c:ising-model) at inverse temperature $\beta/2$.

new_concepts.name: random-cluster model
new_concepts.reminder: The random-cluster model weights an edge set $\omega$ by $p^{|\omega|}(1-p)^{|E\setminus\omega|}q^{k(\omega)}$, with $k(\omega)$ the number of clusters.
new_concepts.definition: The random-cluster model on a finite [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$ with parameters $p\in[0,1]$ and $q>0$ is the probability measure on edge sets $\omega\subseteq E$ given by $\phi_{p,q}(\omega)=Z^{-1}p^{|\omega|}(1-p)^{|E\setminus\omega|}q^{k(\omega)}$. Here $k(\omega)$ is the number of [connected components](c:connected-component) of $(V,\omega)$, isolated vertices included. For $q=1$ it is [Bernoulli percolation](c:percolation), and for integer $q\ge2$ the Edwards–Sokal coupling links it to the [Potts model](c:potts-model) with $p=1-e^{-\beta}$.

statement: In [Bernoulli percolation](c:percolation) on $\mathbb{Z}^d$, there is almost surely at most one infinite open [cluster](c:connected-component). If $\theta(p) > 0$, there is almost surely exactly one.

hypotheses.text: The edges of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ are open [independently](c:independence) with the same probability $p \in [0,1]$.
The lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is invariant under [translations](c:translation), and its boxes satisfy $|\partial\Lambda_n|/|\Lambda_n| \to 0$.

conclusion: The number $N$ of infinite clusters satisfies $\mathbb{P}_p(N \le 1) = 1$, and $\mathbb{P}_p(N = 1) = 1$ when $\theta(p) > 0$.

proofs.name: Burton-Keane trifurcation argument
proofs.slogan: Infinitely many infinite clusters would create trifurcations at positive density, but a box can hold no more trifurcations than boundary vertices.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $p \in (0,1)$. The cases $p = 0$ and $p = 1$ are trivial.

roles.why: Independence lets the proof change the edges of a finite set at a positive cost and makes translations measure preserving.
The ratio of boundary to volume of boxes tends to zero, which defeats a positive density of trifurcations.

steps.slogan: Show by [ergodicity](c:ergodicity) that the number of infinite clusters is almost surely constant.
steps.detail: Approximate a translation-invariant event by an event on finitely many edges, shift the approximation far away, and use independence. This gives $\mathbb{P}(A) = \mathbb{P}(A)^2$, so each event $\{N = k\}$ has probability 0 or 1.

steps.slogan: Merge finitely many infinite clusters by opening every edge of a large box.
steps.detail: If $N = k$ with $2 \le k < \infty$, all infinite clusters meet a box $\Lambda_n$ with probability at least $1/2$. Opening the edges of the box costs a factor $p^{|E_n|}$ and leaves one infinite cluster, which contradicts $N = k$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Build a trifurcation inside a ball from three infinite clusters that reach its sphere.
steps.detail: If $N = \infty$, three infinite clusters of the configuration outside an $\ell^1$ ball reach its sphere. Opening exactly the edges of a [tree](c:tree) in the ball that joins the three entry points makes its branch vertex a trifurcation, so $\mathbb{P}(0 \text{ is a trifurcation}) > 0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the number of trifurcations in a finite graph by the number of boundary vertices.
steps.detail: If every vertex of $T$ splits a connected finite graph into at least three parts that meet $Y$, then $|T| \le |Y| - 2$. Induction removes one vertex of $T$ and applies the bound to each part with the removed vertex added to $Y$.

steps.slogan: Compare the expected number of trifurcations in a box with its boundary size.
steps.detail: The lemma gives at most $|\partial\Lambda_n|$ trifurcations in $\Lambda_{n-1}$, while the [expected value](c:expected-value) of their number is $|\Lambda_{n-1}|\,\mathbb{P}(0 \text{ is a trifurcation})$. The ratio tends to zero, so $N = \infty$ is impossible.

steps.slogan: Combine the excluded cases and use $\theta(p) > 0$ to fix the constant at one.
steps.detail: The constant value of $N$ is 0 or 1. When $\theta(p) > 0$, the event $N \ge 1$ has positive probability, so the constant is 1 and the infinite cluster is unique.

statement: For [bond percolation](c:percolation) on the square lattice, the [critical probability](c:critical-probability) equals $1/2$, and there is no infinite cluster at $p = 1/2$.

hypotheses.text: The graph is the square lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$, a [planar graph](c:planar-graph) whose dual is a translate of itself.
The edges are open [independently](c:independence) with the same probability $p$.

proofs.name: Self-duality with sharpness
proofs.slogan: At $p = 1/2$ a square crossing has probability exactly one half, which forbids both percolation and exponential decay at that point.
proofs.scope: Outline of the whole theorem. The duality of crossings and Proposition 4.1 are taken from the source.

roles.why: Self-duality of the square lattice makes the left-right crossing and the dual top-bottom crossing equally likely at $p = 1/2$.
Independence gives the dual law $\mathbb{P}_{1-p}$, the Harris inequality and the sharpness theorem.

steps.slogan: Show that a near-square crossing has probability exactly one half at $p = 1/2$.
steps.detail: The rectangle $[0,n] \times [0,n-1]$ has no open left-right [path](c:path) exactly when its dual has an open top-bottom dual path. Rotation maps one event to the other, and the dual law at $p = 1/2$ is again $\mathbb{P}_{1/2}$.

steps.slogan: Show that percolation forces crossing probabilities to tend to one.
steps.detail: The square-root trick with the Harris inequality joins boxes near the centre to the left and right sides with high probability. Uniqueness of the infinite cluster then joins the two connections, so $\mathbb{P}_p(H_n) \to 1$ when $\theta(p) > 0$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that there is no percolation at $p = 1/2$, so $p_c \ge 1/2$.
steps.detail: Percolation at $p = 1/2$ would push the crossing probability to one, but self-duality fixes it at one half. So $\theta(1/2) = 0$, and monotonicity gives $\theta(p) = 0$ for $p \le 1/2$.

steps.slogan: Use exponential decay below $p_c$ to exclude $p_c > 1/2$.
steps.detail: Below $p_c$ the sharpness theorem gives $\mathbb{P}_p(H_n) \le n e^{-c_p n} \to 0$. If $p_c$ were above $1/2$, this would hold at $p = 1/2$, against the value one half.

steps.slogan: Combine both bounds to get the exact [critical probability](c:critical-probability) and no percolation there.
steps.detail: The two previous steps give $p_c = 1/2$, and the step before them gives $\theta(p_c) = 0$. A union bound over vertices then excludes any infinite cluster at $p_c$.

new_concepts.name: critical probability
new_concepts.reminder: The critical probability $p_c$ is the threshold above which Bernoulli percolation has an infinite open cluster.
new_concepts.definition: For [Bernoulli percolation](c:percolation) on an infinite connected graph $G$, let $\theta(p)$ be the probability that a fixed vertex lies in an infinite open cluster. The critical probability is $p_c(G)=\sup\{p\in[0,1]:\theta(p)=0\}$. By the Kolmogorov zero-one law, an infinite open cluster exists with probability $0$ when $p<p_c$ and with probability $1$ when $p>p_c$.

statement: For a Bernoulli [product measure](c:product-measure) on $\{0,1\}^E$ with $E$ finite and two [increasing events](c:increasing-event) $A$ and $B$, the probability that $A$ and $B$ occur on disjoint sets of coordinates is at most $\mathbb{P}(A)\,\mathbb{P}(B)$.

hypotheses.text: The set $E$ is finite and the coordinates $\omega_e$ are [independent](c:independence) [Bernoulli](c:bernoulli-distribution) variables with $\mathbb{P}(\omega_e = 1) = p_e$.
The events $A$ and $B$ are [increasing](c:increasing-event).

conclusion: $\mathbb{P}(A \circ B) \le \mathbb{P}(A)\,\mathbb{P}(B)$, where $A \circ B$ is the event that $A$ and $B$ have disjoint witnesses.

proofs.name: Duplication and one-coordinate swaps
proofs.slogan: Move the coordinates that $A$ reads, one at a time, to an independent copy, and check that each move can only raise the probability.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for increasing events on a finite product space.

roles.why: Independence lets the proof replace one coordinate by an independent copy with the same law, and the copies make the last event a product.
Monotonicity reduces witnesses to sets of open coordinates, which the swap argument moves between the copies.

steps.slogan: Reduce the witnesses of an increasing event to sets of open coordinates.
steps.detail: For an [increasing event](c:increasing-event) $C$, a set $K$ of open coordinates is a witness exactly when the configuration $1_K$ is in $C$, and every witness stays a witness after removal of its closed coordinates.

steps.slogan: Build an independent copy and interpolate the coordinates that $A$ reads.
steps.detail: Take an independent copy $\omega'$ and let $\omega^{(j)}$ use $\omega'_i$ for $i < j$ and $\omega_i$ for $i \ge j$. With $\hat A_j = \{\omega^{(j)} \in A\}$ and $\hat B = \{\omega \in B\}$, the first event $\hat A_1 \circ \hat B$ has probability $\mathbb{P}(A \circ B)$ and the last has probability $\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)$ by [independence](c:independence).

steps.slogan: Compare two neighbouring events by a three-case analysis of one coordinate pair.
steps.detail: Fix all coordinates except $x = \omega_j$ and $y = \omega'_j$. The event $\hat A_j \circ \hat B$ depends on $x$ only. If it needs $x = 1$ and the witness of $A$ uses $(j,1)$, move that coordinate to $(j,2)$. Then $\hat A_{j+1} \circ \hat B$ holds when $y = 1$, which has the same [conditional probability](c:conditional-probability) $p_j$.

steps.slogan: Average the one-swap comparisons and chain them from the first event to the last.
steps.detail: The law of total probability turns each conditional comparison into $\hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat A_j \circ \hat B) \le \hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat A_{j+1} \circ \hat B)$, and the $N$ inequalities chain to $\mathbb{P}(A \circ B) \le \mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)$.

concepts.c:conditional-probability: Each swap is compared conditionally on all other coordinates.

new_concepts.reminder: An event is increasing when opening more edges can never destroy it.
new_concepts.definition: Order $\Omega=\{0,1\}^E$ coordinatewise, so $\omega\le\omega'$ when $\omega(e)\le\omega'(e)$ for every edge $e$. An event $A\subseteq\Omega$ is increasing if $\omega\in A$ and $\omega\le\omega'$ imply $\omega'\in A$, and it is decreasing if its complement is increasing. For [Bernoulli percolation](c:percolation), the Harris–FKG inequality says that two increasing events are positively correlated.

statement: For a Bernoulli [product measure](c:product-measure) on $\{0,1\}^E$ with $E$ finite and an [increasing event](c:increasing-event) $A$, the [derivative](c:derivative) of $p \mapsto \mathbb{P}_p(A)$ equals the expected number of edges that are pivotal for $A$.

hypotheses.text: The set $E$ is finite and the coordinates $\omega_e$ are [independent](c:independence) [Bernoulli](c:bernoulli-distribution) variables with $\mathbb{P}_p(\omega_e = 1) = p_e$.
The event $A$ is [increasing](c:increasing-event): $\omega \in A$ and $\omega \le \omega'$ give $\omega' \in A$.

conclusion: $\partial \mathbb{P}_p(A) / \partial p_e = \mathbb{P}_p(\mathrm{Piv}_e(A))$ for each $e$, and with all $p_e = p$, $\frac{d}{dp}\mathbb{P}_p(A) = \sum_{e \in E} \mathbb{P}_p(\mathrm{Piv}_e(A))$.

proofs.name: Conditioning on one edge
proofs.slogan: The probability of $A$ is affine in each $p_e$, and its slope in $p_e$ is the probability that $e$ is pivotal.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every finite $E$, every parameter vector in $[0,1]^E$ and every increasing event $A$.

roles.why: Independence makes the events $\{\omega^e \in A\}$ and $\{\omega_e \in A\}$ independent of $\omega_e$, and finiteness makes $\mathbb{P}_p(A)$ a [polynomial](c:polynomial).
Monotonicity gives $\{\omega_e \in A\} \subseteq \{\omega^e \in A\}$, so the slope is the probability of the difference, which is the pivotal event.

steps.slogan: Write the probability of $A$ as a polynomial that is affine in each parameter.
steps.detail: Expand $\mathbb{P}_p(A) = \sum_{\omega \in A} \prod_{e} p_e^{\omega_e}(1-p_e)^{1-\omega_e}$. Each product contains $p_e$ or $1-p_e$ once, so the sum is a [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree at most one in each $p_e$.

steps.slogan: Split the probability of $A$ according to the state of one edge.
steps.detail: Let $B^+ = \{\omega^e \in A\}$ and $B^- = \{\omega_e \in A\}$. Both depend only on edges other than $e$, so [independence](c:independence) gives $\mathbb{P}_p(A) = p_e\,\mathbb{P}_p(B^+) + (1-p_e)\,\mathbb{P}_p(B^-)$, where the two probabilities do not depend on $p_e$.

steps.slogan: Identify the slope in $p_e$ with the probability that the edge $e$ is pivotal.
steps.detail: The slope is $\mathbb{P}_p(B^+) - \mathbb{P}_p(B^-)$. Because $A$ is increasing and $\omega_e \le \omega^e$, we have $B^- \subseteq B^+$. The difference $B^+ \setminus B^-$ is the event $\mathrm{Piv}_e(A)$ that $e$ is pivotal.

steps.slogan: Set all parameters equal and sum the partial derivatives with the chain rule.
steps.detail: With $f(p) = g(p, \dots, p)$ and $g$ a polynomial, the chain rule gives $f'(p) = \sum_e \partial_e g(p,\dots,p) = \sum_e \mathbb{P}_p(\mathrm{Piv}_e(A))$. Linearity of the [expected value](c:expected-value) turns this sum into the mean number of pivotal edges.

proofs.name: Reflection of the right-most crossing
proofs.slogan: Reflect the right-most vertical crossing of a square to build a symmetric barrier, then glue crossings with the Harris inequality.
proofs.scope: Outline of the whole theorem. The self-duality of crossings of squares is taken from the source.

roles.why: At $p = 1/2$ the dual configuration has the same law, which fixes square crossings at one half and gives the upper bound.

steps.slogan: Bound square crossing probabilities below by one half with self-duality.
steps.detail: The near-square $[0,n] \times [0,n-1]$ is crossed with probability exactly $1/2$ by self-duality. A square contains it, so horizontal and vertical crossings of squares have probability at least $1/2$.

steps.slogan: Condition on the right-most vertical crossing of the square $[0,n]^2$.
steps.detail: The event that the right-most crossing equals $\gamma$ depends only on edges on and to the right of $\gamma$. So the region to the left of $\gamma$ and its reflection keeps independent edges, by [conditional probability](c:conditional-probability) and independence.

steps.slogan: Join the crossing to the far left side with probability one quarter using reflection symmetry.
steps.detail: A left-right crossing of $[-n,n]^2$ must hit the symmetric [path](c:path) $\gamma \cup \sigma(\gamma)$. Reflection makes a hit on $\gamma$ and a hit on $\sigma(\gamma)$ equally likely, so each has probability at least $1/4$, and $\mathbb{P}(B) \ge 1/8$.

steps.slogan: Glue a square crossing with two arm events to cross a $3n \times 2n$ rectangle.
steps.detail: A horizontal crossing of the square meets both vertical crossings, which are joined to the left and right sides of $[-n,2n] \times [-n,n]$. The Harris inequality multiplies $1/2$, $1/8$ and $1/8$ to give $1/128$.

steps.slogan: Chain overlapping rectangles to reach every aspect ratio.
steps.detail: Overlapping rectangles of ratio $3/2$ with square overlaps link into a long rectangle, because their crossings meet the vertical crossings of the overlaps. The Harris inequality gives a lower bound that depends only on the number of rectangles.

steps.slogan: Get the upper bound from a dual crossing in the other direction.
steps.detail: A rectangle has no horizontal crossing exactly when its dual has a vertical dual crossing. At $p = 1/2$ this has the law of a crossing of a rectangle with ratio near $1/\rho$, which the lower bound controls.

statement: For [Bernoulli percolation](c:percolation) on $\mathbb{Z}^d$, connection probabilities decay exponentially fast below the [critical probability](c:critical-probability) $p_c$, and $\theta(p) \ge (p-p_c)/(p(1-p_c))$ above $p_c$. So the [phase transition](c:phase-transition) is sharp.

hypotheses.text: The edges of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, $d \ge 2$, are open [independently](c:independence) with the same probability $p$.

conclusion: For $p < p_c$, $\mathbb{P}_p(0 \leftrightarrow \partial\Lambda_n) \le e^{-c_p n}$ for all $n \ge 1$. For $p > p_c$, $\theta(p) \ge (p - p_c)/(p(1-p_c))$. Also $p_c = \sup\{p : \varphi_p(S) < 1 \text{ for some finite } S \ni 0\}$.

proofs.name: Duminil-Copin and Tassion argument
proofs.slogan: A finite set with $\varphi_p(S) < 1$ forces exponential decay, and its absence forces a differential inequality that makes $\theta$ grow linearly.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for bond percolation on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with $d \ge 2$.

roles.why: Independence of edges lets the proof factor events on disjoint edge sets, and the common parameter makes the Russo formula a derivative in $p$.

steps.slogan: Show that one finite set $S$ with $\varphi_p(S) < 1$ gives exponential decay.
steps.detail: Decompose a path from $0$ to $\partial\Lambda_n$ at its last vertex in the cluster of $0$ inside $S$. [Independence](c:independence) of three disjoint edge sets gives $\theta_n \le \varphi_p(S)\,\theta_{n-L}$, and iteration gives $\theta_{kL} \le \varphi_p(S)^k$.

steps.slogan: Write the derivative of $\theta_n$ as a sum over closed [pivotal](c:increasing-event) edges.
steps.detail: The Russo-Margulis formula and independence of the pivotal event from the edge state give $\theta_n' = (1-p)^{-1}\sum \mathbb{P}_p(0 \leftrightarrow x,\ y \leftrightarrow \partial\Lambda_n,\ 0 \not\leftrightarrow \partial\Lambda_n)$ over ordered neighbouring pairs in the box.

steps.slogan: Condition on the set of vertices not joined to the boundary to get $\theta_n' = \mathbb{E}_p[\varphi_p(\mathcal{S})]/(p(1-p))$.
steps.detail: The event $\{\mathcal{S} = S\}$ depends only on edges with an endpoint outside $S$, and the connection $0 \leftrightarrow x$ inside $S$ depends only on edges inside $S$. Their independence turns the sum of the previous step into the [expected value](c:expected-value) of $\varphi_p(\mathcal{S})$.

steps.slogan: Prove exponential decay below the threshold $\tilde p_c$ defined by the finite criterion.
steps.detail: The function $\varphi_p(S)$ is nondecreasing in $p$ by the Russo-Margulis formula. So every $p < \tilde p_c$ has a finite $S$ with $\varphi_p(S) < 1$, and the finite criterion gives decay and $\theta(p) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the differential inequality above $\tilde p_c$ to get the mean-field lower bound.
steps.detail: Above $\tilde p_c$ every $S \ni 0$ has $\varphi_p(S) \ge 1$, so $\theta_n' \ge (1-\theta_n)/(p(1-p))$. The [derivative](c:derivative) bound integrates to $\theta_n(p) \ge (p - \tilde p_c)/(p(1-\tilde p_c))$, and $n \to \infty$ gives the same bound for $\theta$.

steps.slogan: Identify $\tilde p_c$ with $p_c$ and collect the three conclusions.
steps.detail: Decay below $\tilde p_c$ gives $\tilde p_c \le p_c$, and positivity of $\theta$ above $\tilde p_c$ gives $p_c \le \tilde p_c$. So the two thresholds agree and both bounds hold with $p_c$.

new_concepts.name: critical probability
new_concepts.reminder: The critical probability $p_c$ is the threshold above which Bernoulli percolation has an infinite open cluster.
new_concepts.definition: For [Bernoulli percolation](c:percolation) on an infinite connected graph $G$, let $\theta(p)$ be the probability that a fixed vertex lies in an infinite open cluster. The critical probability is $p_c(G)=\sup\{p\in[0,1]:\theta(p)=0\}$. By the Kolmogorov zero-one law, an infinite open cluster exists with probability $0$ when $p<p_c$ and with probability $1$ when $p>p_c$.

new_concepts.name: free energy
new_concepts.reminder: The free energy is $-1/\beta$ times the pressure $\psi=\lim|\Lambda|^{-1}\log Z_\Lambda$ of a lattice model.
new_concepts.definition: For a lattice spin model with [partition function](c:partition-function) $Z_\Lambda(\beta)$ in a finite box $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$, the pressure is the [thermodynamic limit](c:thermodynamic-limit) $\psi(\beta)=\lim_{\Lambda\uparrow\mathbb Z^d}|\Lambda|^{-1}\log Z_\Lambda(\beta)$. The free energy per site is $f(\beta)=-\psi(\beta)/\beta$, where $\beta$ is the [inverse temperature](c:inverse-temperature). For finite-range interactions, the limit exists along boxes, it does not depend on the boundary condition, and $\psi$ is convex.

new_concepts.name: Gibbs measure
new_concepts.reminder: A Gibbs measure is an infinite-volume law whose conditional law in each finite box is the finite Gibbs distribution.
new_concepts.definition: For finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$ and a [boundary condition](c:boundary-condition) $\eta$, let $\pi_\Lambda^\eta$ be the finite-volume [Gibbs distribution](c:gibbs-distribution) of an interaction in $\Lambda$, with the spins outside $\Lambda$ fixed to $\eta$. A [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu$ on the configuration space $S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ is a Gibbs measure if, for every finite $\Lambda$, the [conditional distribution](c:conditional-distribution) of the spins in $\Lambda$ given the spins outside $\Lambda$ is $\pi_\Lambda^\eta$ for $\mu$-almost every outside configuration $\eta$. These conditions are the DLR equations.

new_concepts.definition: The inverse temperature of a system at absolute temperature $T$ is $\beta=1/(k_BT)$, where $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant. It is the parameter in the [Boltzmann distribution](c:boltzmann-distribution) $\mu_\beta(\sigma)=e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}/Z(\beta)$ of a [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) $H$. new_concepts.definition: A phase transition of a lattice model is a value of its parameters, such as the inverse temperature $\beta$ and the field $h$, at which the infinite-volume [free energy](c:free-energy) is not real-analytic. It is first-order when a first derivative of the free energy is discontinuous there. statement: For [bond percolation](c:percolation) on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with $d \ge 2$, the [critical probability](c:critical-probability) satisfies $1/(2d-1) \le p_c(d) \le 5/6$, so $0 < p_c(d) < 1$.

hypotheses.text: The dimension satisfies $d \ge 2$.
Each edge of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is open with probability $p$, [independently](c:independence) of the other edges.

proofs.name: Path counting and dual circuits
proofs.slogan: Few open long paths exist when $p$ is small, and few closed dual circuits exist when $p$ is close to 1.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The upper bound is proved on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and transferred to $\mathbb{Z}^d$ through a plane.

roles.why: The lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with $d \ge 2$ contains a copy of $\mathbb{Z}^2$, where planar duality is available.
Independence gives probability $p^n$ to an open path and $(1-p)^n$ to a closed circuit of $n$ distinct edges.

steps.slogan: Bound the percolation probability by the number of open [self-avoiding walks](c:self-avoiding-walk) of length $n$.
steps.detail: An infinite cluster contains an open self-avoiding walk of every length $n$ from the origin. There are at most $2d(2d-1)^{n-1}$ such walks, so $\theta_d(p) \le 2d(2d-1)^{n-1}p^n$, which tends to $0$ when $p < 1/(2d-1)$.

steps.slogan: Compare percolation on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with percolation on one plane.
steps.detail: The edges of the plane $\mathbb{Z}^2 \times \{0\}$ form an independent bond percolation on $\mathbb{Z}^2$, and an infinite cluster there is infinite in $\mathbb{Z}^d$. So $\theta_d(p) \ge \theta_2(p)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the dual boundary of a finite cluster is an even graph with an odd crossing count.
steps.detail: The duals of the boundary edges of the finite [cluster](c:connected-component) $C$ are all open. Each dual vertex sees an even number of them, because membership in $C$ changes an even number of times around a unit square, and an odd number cross the positive $x$-axis.

steps.slogan: Extract one closed dual [cycle](c:cycle) of length $n$ that crosses the positive axis within distance $n/2$.
steps.detail: An even graph splits into edge-disjoint cycles, so one cycle crosses the positive axis an odd number of times. A closed dual walk crosses the $x$-axis an even number of times, so the cycle crosses the negative axis too, and its length is at least $2(k+1)$.

steps.slogan: Sum the probabilities of all candidate dual cycles with the union bound.
steps.detail: At most $n$ crossing positions and at most $3^n$ cycles of length $n$ through each give $1 - \theta_2(p) \le \sum_{n \ge 4} n(3(1-p))^n$, which is at most $5/8$ when $p \ge 5/6$.

steps.slogan: Combine the lower and upper estimates into bounds on the critical probability.
steps.detail: The first step gives $\theta_d = 0$ below $1/(2d-1)$, and the plane comparison with the circuit count gives $\theta_d \ge 3/8$ above $5/6$. The definition of $p_c(d)$ as an infimum then gives both bounds.

new_concepts.reminder: A self-avoiding walk is a nearest-neighbor path on a lattice that never visits the same vertex twice.
new_concepts.definition: An $n$-step self-avoiding walk on a [graph](c:graph) $G$ from a vertex $x$ is a sequence of vertices $(\omega_0,\dots,\omega_n)$ with $\omega_0=x$, with $\omega_{i-1}\omega_i$ an edge for each $i$, and with $\omega_i\ne\omega_j$ for $i\ne j$. proofs.name: Smirnov's observable in Khristoforov's version
proofs.slogan: Combine three crossing probabilities with cube roots of unity into an observable that is discretely holomorphic and converges to the conformal map onto the triangle.
proofs.scope: Outline of the whole theorem. The local relation and the Hölder bound are taken from the source.

roles.why: At $p = 1/2$ all colourings have the same weight, so the observable counts loop configurations, and the crossing bounds of RSW hold.
A Jordan domain has a conformal map onto the triangle that extends to the boundary and is fixed by three boundary points.

steps.slogan: Encode colourings of hexagons as loop configurations on the hexagonal lattice.
steps.detail: Edges between hexagons of different colours form an even subgraph, and this is a bijection onto loop configurations. Paths between marked mid-edges then encode crossing events.

steps.slogan: Define the observable with cube roots of unity and show that it takes values in the triangle.
steps.detail: With $F = F_a + jF_b + j^2F_c$ and $F_a + F_b + F_c = 1$, the value of $F$ is a convex combination of the vertices of $T$. On each boundary arc one term vanishes, so the boundary goes to the matching side of the triangle.

steps.slogan: Show that discrete [contour integrals](c:contour-integral) of the observable vanish.
steps.detail: Grouping configurations in triples around a vertex gives $(p-v)F(p) + (q-v)F(q) + (r-v)F(r) = 0$, because the three contributions differ by [roots of unity](c:root-of-unity) that sum to zero. Summing over triangles gives vanishing integrals on every closed lattice contour.

steps.slogan: Prove a uniform Hölder bound and extract convergent subsequences.
steps.detail: The observable is the probability that an interface does not separate $z$ from $a$. Crossing bounds in annuli give a Hölder modulus that does not depend on the mesh, and the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem gives uniform limits on compact sets.

steps.slogan: Identify every subsequential limit with the conformal map onto the triangle.
steps.detail: Vanishing contour integrals pass to the limit, so Morera's theorem makes the limit a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function). It maps the three arcs onto the three sides with $a, b, c \mapsto 1, j, j^2$, so boundary correspondence forces it to equal $\varphi$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the limit at the fourth point to read off the crossing probability.
steps.detail: On the arc from $c$ to $a$ the observable equals $F_a + j^2(1-F_a)$, where $F_a(d_\delta)$ is the crossing probability. Convergence to $\varphi(d) = x + j^2(1-x)$ gives the limit $x$.

new_concepts.definition: Bernoulli bond percolation with parameter $p\in[0,1]$ on a [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$ declares each edge open with probability $p$ and closed otherwise, independently of all other edges. Its law is the [product measure](c:product-measure) $\mathbb P_p=\bigotimes_{e\in E}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ on $\{0,1\}^E$. The open clusters are the [connected components](c:connected-component) of the graph $(V,\{e:\omega(e)=1\})$, and site percolation does the same with vertices.

statement: On the hexagonal lattice, the [connective constant](c:connective-constant) of [self-avoiding walks](c:self-avoiding-walk) is $\mu = \sqrt{2+\sqrt{2}}$.

hypotheses.text: The [graph](c:graph) is the hexagonal lattice $\mathbb{H}$, a [planar graph](c:planar-graph) in which every vertex has three neighbours.
$c_n$ counts the $n$-step [self-avoiding walks](c:self-avoiding-walk) on $\mathbb{H}$ that start at a fixed vertex.

proofs.name: Holomorphic observable on strips
proofs.slogan: A complex walk observable cancels locally at $z_c = 1/\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2}}$, which gives an exact identity on strips that bounds bridges from above and below.
proofs.scope: Outline of the whole theorem. The equality of the bridge growth rate and $\mu$ on $\mathbb{H}$, the pairing of walks and the boundary windings are taken from the source.

roles.why: Around each vertex the three mid-edges differ by cube roots of unity, and the lattice has strips with straight sides and a reflection symmetry.
The walk counts form the generating functions $\chi$ and $B$, whose radius of convergence is $1/\mu$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the theorem to two facts about the bridge generating function.
steps.detail: Bridges grow at the same rate as all walks, so the [radius of convergence](c:radius-of-convergence) of the bridge [generating function](c:generating-function) $B$ is $1/\mu$. It is sufficient to show $B(z)<\infty$ for $z<z_c$, and $B(z_c)=\infty$ or $\chi(z_c)=\infty$.

steps.slogan: Define the walk observable and show that it cancels around every vertex.
steps.detail: The observable sums $e^{-i\sigma W}z^{\ell}$ over walks from a boundary mid-edge. Walks that end around a vertex form pairs and triplets. With the cube [root of unity](c:root-of-unity) $j$ and $\sigma=5/8$, the pair factor $j\bar\lambda^4+\bar j\lambda^4$ is zero. The triplet factor $1-2z\cos(\pi/8)$ is zero exactly at $z=z_c$.

steps.slogan: Add the local relation over a strip to get an exact boundary identity.
steps.detail: The terms of interior mid-edges cancel, and only the four sides of the strip remain. Their fixed windings and the [reflection](c:reflection) in the horizontal line through $a$ give $1=c_\alpha A_{T,L}+B_{T,L}+c_\varepsilon E_{T,L}$ at $z_c$.

steps.slogan: Show that the bridge series converges for every $z$ below $z_c$.
steps.detail: The identity gives $B_T(z_c)\le 1$ in the limit $L\to\infty$. A bridge of span $T$ has at least $T$ vertices, so $B_T(z)\le (z/z_c)^T$. The sum over $T$ is a convergent geometric series.

steps.slogan: Show that walks to the strip ends make the susceptibility infinite.
steps.detail: If $E_T(z_c)>0$ for some $T$, then $E_{T,L}(z_c)\ge E_T(z_c)$ for every $L$. Walks that end at different heights are different, so $\chi(z_c)\ge\sum_L E_T(z_c)=\infty$.

steps.slogan: Bound bridges below by $m/T$ when no walk reaches the strip ends.
steps.detail: If every $E_T(z_c)$ is zero, then $1=c_\alpha A_T+B_T$. A cut of each new walk in $A_{T+1}$ gives two bridges, so $c_\alpha K B_{T+1}^2+B_{T+1}\ge B_T$ for a constant $K>0$. Induction gives $B_T\ge m/T$, so $B(z_c)=\infty$.

steps.slogan: Combine both bounds to identify the [connective constant](c:connective-constant) as $\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2}}$.
steps.detail: Convergence below $z_c$ gives $\mu\le 1/z_c$. Divergence of $B$ or $\chi$ at $z_c$ gives $\mu\ge 1/z_c$. So $\mu=1/z_c=2\cos(\pi/8)=\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2}}$.

new_concepts.name: connective constant
new_concepts.reminder: The connective constant $\mu=\lim c_n^{1/n}$ is the exponential growth rate of the number of self-avoiding walks.
new_concepts.definition: Let $c_n$ be the number of $n$-step [self-avoiding walks](c:self-avoiding-walk) from a fixed vertex of a vertex-transitive graph such as $\mathbb Z^d$. Since $c_{n+m}\le c_nc_m$, Fekete's lemma shows that the limit $\mu=\lim_{n\to\infty}c_n^{1/n}$ exists and equals $\inf_nc_n^{1/n}$. This limit is the connective constant.

new_concepts.name: self-avoiding walk
new_concepts.reminder: A self-avoiding walk is a nearest-neighbor path on a lattice that never visits the same vertex twice.
new_concepts.definition: An $n$-step self-avoiding walk on a [graph](c:graph) $G$ from a vertex $x$ is a sequence of vertices $(\omega_0,\dots,\omega_n)$ with $\omega_0=x$, with $\omega_{i-1}\omega_i$ an edge for each $i$, and with $\omega_i\ne\omega_j$ for $i\ne j$. Let $c_n$ be the number of such walks. The uniform measure on them is a model of a linear polymer, usually on $\mathbb Z^d$.

statement: The number $c_n$ of $n$-step [self-avoiding walks](c:self-avoiding-walk) on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ satisfies $c_n \le b_{n+1} e^{\pi\sqrt{2(n+1)/3}} \le \mu^{n+1} e^{\pi\sqrt{2(n+1)/3}}$, where $b_n$ counts bridges and $\mu$ is the [connective constant](c:connective-constant).

hypotheses.text: The walks are nearest-neighbour [self-avoiding walks](c:self-avoiding-walk) on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with $d \ge 1$, started at $0$.
The [connective constant](c:connective-constant) $\mu = \lim_n c_n^{1/n}$ exists because $c_{n+m} \le c_n c_m$.

conclusion: $c_n \le b_{n+1} e^{\pi\sqrt{2(n+1)/3}} \le \mu^{n+1} e^{\pi\sqrt{2(n+1)/3}}$ for every $n \ge 0$, and $b_n^{1/n} \to \mu$.

proofs.name: Unfolding into bridges
proofs.slogan: Cut a walk at its last leftmost point into two half-space walks, unfold each into a bridge by reflections, and count the unfoldings with partitions.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for every $d \ge 1$ and every $n \ge 0$, with an explicit constant in place of the Hardy-Ramanujan asymptotics.

roles.why: Reflections in hyperplanes of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and concatenation keep walks self-avoiding when the pieces lie in disjoint half-spaces.
The limit $\mu$ bounds $b_n^{1/n}$ through $b_n^k \le c_{kn}$.

steps.slogan: Concatenate bridges to show $b_{n+m} \ge b_n b_m$ and $b_n \le \mu^n$.
steps.detail: A bridge stays at first coordinate at most its end value, and a second bridge started at that end stays strictly above it. So concatenation is injective into bridges, and $b_n^k \le b_{kn} \le c_{kn}$ gives $b_n \le \mu^n$.

steps.slogan: Split a walk at its last leftmost point into two half-space walks.
steps.detail: Cutting at the last time $m$ where the first coordinate is minimal gives a half-space walk after $m$ and, with the extra point $\omega(m) - e_1$, a reversed half-space walk before $m$. So $c_n \le \sum_m h_{n-m} h_{m+1}$.

steps.slogan: Unfold a half-space walk into a bridge by reflections at its successive extremes.
steps.detail: The spans $A_1 > A_2 > \dots > A_K > 0$ between successive last extremes form an [integer partition](c:integer-partition) into distinct parts. Reflecting the walk after its first extreme merges $A_1$ and $A_2$ injectively, so $h_n \le P_D(n)\, b_n$.

steps.slogan: Bound the convolution of distinct-part partition counts with a [generating function](c:generating-function).
steps.detail: The sum $\sum_{a+b=N} P_D(a)P_D(b)$ is at most $x^{-N}\prod_k(1+x^k)^2$. Euler's identity, AM-GM and $\sum 1/j^2 = \pi^2/6$ give $\log\prod_k(1+x^k) \le \pi^2/(12 s)$ for $x = e^{-s}$, and $s = \pi/\sqrt{6N}$ gives $e^{\pi\sqrt{2N/3}}$.

steps.slogan: Combine the split, the unfolding and supermultiplicativity into the final bound on $c_n$.
steps.detail: The two previous bounds give $c_n \le \sum_m P_D(n-m)P_D(m+1)\, b_{n-m} b_{m+1} \le b_{n+1}\, e^{\pi\sqrt{2(n+1)/3}}$, and $b_{n+1} \le \mu^{n+1}$. Taking $(n+1)$-th roots shows $b_n^{1/n} \to \mu$.

concepts.c:self-avoiding-walk: Self-avoiding walks are the objects that the bound counts.
concepts.c:connective-constant: The connective constant is the exponential growth rate of $c_n$ and $b_n$.
concepts.c:integer-partition: The spans of an unfolded walk form a partition into distinct parts.
concepts.c:generating-function: The generating function of distinct-part partitions gives the explicit subexponential factor.

statement: For the [self-avoiding walk](c:self-avoiding-walk) on $\mathbb Z^d$ with $d \ge 5$, $c_n = A\mu^n[1 + O(n^{-\varepsilon})]$ with $\mu$ the [connective constant](c:connective-constant), $E_n|\omega(n)|^2 = Dn[1 + O(n^{-\varepsilon})]$, and the rescaled walk $\omega(\lfloor n\,\cdot\rfloor)/\sqrt{Dn}$ [converges in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion).

The dimension satisfies $d \ge 5$, above the upper critical dimension $4$.

conclusion: The self-avoiding walk has the same critical behaviour as simple [random walk](c:random-walk): $\gamma = 1$, $\nu = 1/2$, and a Brownian scaling limit.

proofs.name: Lace expansion with a bootstrap argument
proofs.slogan: Expand self-intersections into small diagrams, show by a bootstrap that the walk stays close to simple random walk, then read off the asymptotics.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline. The computer-assisted bounds for $d = 5, 6, \dots$ and the transfer from [generating functions](c:generating-function) to coefficients are cited from Hara and Slade.

roles.why: Inclusion-exclusion on self-intersections of the walk produces the lace expansion.
Above four dimensions the random-walk bubble integral is finite, and for $d \ge 5$ it is small enough to close the bootstrap.

steps.slogan: Write the two-point function with the lace expansion in [Fourier](c:fourier-transform) variables.
steps.detail: Inclusion-exclusion gives $\hat G_z(k) = 1/(1 - 2dz\hat D(k) - \hat\Pi_z(k))$, where $\hat\Pi_z$ is an alternating sum of diagrams with $N$ loops.

steps.slogan: Bound each lace diagram by powers of the bubble diagram.
steps.detail: Theorem 4.1 of Slade's notes bounds the $N$-loop term by $\|H_z\|_\infty(\|H_z\|_\infty + \|H_z\|_2^2)^{N-1}$, so a small bubble diagram makes $\hat\Pi_z$ small.

steps.slogan: Compare the self-avoiding two-point function with [random walk](c:random-walk) by a continuity bootstrap up to $z_c$.
steps.detail: A continuous function $f$ that compares $\hat G_z$ with the random-walk two-point function cannot jump over the gap between $1 + C\beta$ and $4$. This gives the infrared bound and the bubble condition, with computer-assisted inputs for $d \ge 5$.

steps.slogan: Find the simple pole of the susceptibility [generating function](c:generating-function) at $z_c$.
steps.detail: Since $\chi(z) = 1/(1 - 2dz - \hat\Pi_z(0))$ and the denominator vanishes at $z_c$ with nonzero slope, $\chi(z) \sim A(1 - z/z_c)^{-1}$ with $A = z_c^{-1}[2d + \partial_z\hat\Pi_{z_c}(0)]^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the singular behaviour to $c_n$ and to the rescaled walk.
steps.detail: Hara and Slade turn the generating-function asymptotics into $c_n = A\mu^n[1 + O(n^{-\varepsilon})]$ and $E_n|\omega(n)|^2 = Dn[1 + O(n^{-\varepsilon})]$. Fourier transforms converge to $e^{-|k|^2/(2d)}$, which with tightness gives the [Brownian](c:brownian-motion) limit.

statement: For two independent [random currents](c:random-current) on a finite graph with sources $A$ and $B$, the weighted sum of $F(n_1 + n_2)$ equals the same sum over currents with sources $A \Delta B$ and $\emptyset$, restricted to the event that every [connected component](c:connected-component) of the trace of $n_1 + n_2$ meets $B$ an even number of times.

hypotheses.text: The [graph](c:graph) $G = (V, E)$ is finite and every edge weight satisfies $\beta_e \ge 0$.
The function $F$ on currents is bounded, or nonnegative.

conclusion: $\sum_{\partial n_1 = A,\, \partial n_2 = B} F(n_1+n_2)\, w(n_1) w(n_2) = \sum_{\partial n_1 = A\Delta B,\, \partial n_2 = \emptyset} F(n_1+n_2)\, w(n_1) w(n_2)\, \mathbf{1}[\widehat{n_1+n_2} \in \mathcal{F}_B]$.

proofs.name: Multigraph and path involution
proofs.slogan: Fix the sum of the two currents, count source sets as subsets of a multigraph, and switch sources by a symmetric difference with paths.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma, for every finite graph, all nonnegative weights and all bounded or nonnegative $F$.

roles.why: Finiteness makes $\sum_n w(n) = \prod_e e^{\beta_e}$ finite and gives a finite [multigraph](c:multigraph) for each fixed sum $m$.
A bounded or nonnegative $F$ makes both double series absolutely convergent or nonnegative, so they can be regrouped.

steps.slogan: Regroup both sums by the total current $m = n_1 + n_2$ with binomial factors.
steps.detail: Since $w(n)w(m-n) = w(m)\prod_e \binom{m_e}{n_e}$ and $\partial(n_1+n_2) = \partial n_1 \Delta \partial n_2$, it suffices to compare $\sum_{n \le m,\, \partial n = A} \prod_e \binom{m_e}{n_e}$ with $\mathbf{1}[\hat m \in \mathcal{F}_B]$ times the same sum with $\partial n = A\Delta B$, for each $m$ with $\partial m = A \Delta B$.

steps.slogan: Read the binomial sums as counts of sub-multigraphs with given odd-degree vertices.
steps.detail: Replace each edge $e$ by $m_e$ distinct copies to get a [multigraph](c:multigraph) $M$. Choosing $n_e$ of the copies of each edge gives $\prod_e \binom{m_e}{n_e}$ subsets, so each sum counts the subsets $N \subset M$ whose odd-degree set $\partial N$ is prescribed.

steps.slogan: Show by degree parity that both counts vanish when some component meets $B$ oddly.
steps.detail: Inside a [connected component](c:connected-component) $C$ of $\hat m$ every subset $N$ has an even number of odd-degree vertices by the degree-sum formula. If $|B \cap C|$ is odd, then $|A \cap C|$ is odd, so no $N$ has $\partial N = A$.

steps.slogan: Build a set $K$ of edge copies with sources $B$ from [paths](c:path) inside components.
steps.detail: When every component meets $B$ an even number of times, pair the points of $B$ in each component and join each pair by a simple path in $\hat m$. The [symmetric difference](c:symmetric-difference) $K$ of these paths, with one fixed copy per edge, has $\partial K = B$.

steps.slogan: Switch sources with the [involution](c:involution) $N \mapsto N \Delta K$ and sum back over $m$.
steps.detail: Since $\partial(N \Delta K) = \partial N \Delta B$, the involution maps subsets with sources $A$ bijectively onto subsets with sources $A \Delta B$. With the parity case this proves the identity for each $m$, and summing $F(m)w(m)$ times it over $m$ gives the lemma.

concepts.c:random-current: Random currents are the objects whose sources the lemma switches.
concepts.c:connected-component: The event $\mathcal{F}_B$ is a parity condition on each connected component.
concepts.c:graph: The lemma lives on a finite graph with edge weights.
concepts.c:multigraph: The multigraph of copies turns binomial sums into subset counts.
concepts.c:path: Paths between paired sources give a set of edges with sources $B$.
concepts.c:symmetric-difference: Symmetric difference adds degree parities and combines the paths.
concepts.c:involution: The involution $N \mapsto N \Delta K$ is the bijection that switches sources.

new_concepts.name: random current
new_concepts.reminder: A random current is a random integer-valued function on edges whose odd-degree vertices form a prescribed source set.
new_concepts.definition: For the [Ising model](c:ising-model) on a finite graph $G=(V,E)$ with coupling constants $\beta J_{xy}\ge0$, a current is a function $n:E\to\{0,1,2,\dots\}$, and its source set $\partial n$ is the set of vertices $x$ with $\sum_yn_{xy}$ odd. The weight of $n$ is $w(n)=\prod_{xy\in E}(\beta J_{xy})^{n_{xy}}/n_{xy}!$, and the random current with sources $A$ has law proportional to $w(n)\mathbf 1\{\partial n=A\}$. Expanding each factor $e^{\beta J_{xy}\sigma_x\sigma_y}$ in a power series gives $\langle\prod_{x\in A}\sigma_x\rangle=\sum_{\partial n=A}w(n)/\sum_{\partial n=\emptyset}w(n)$.

statement: For the two-dimensional [Ising model](c:ising-model) at $\beta > \beta_c$, every [Gibbs measure](c:gibbs-measure) is a mixture $\alpha\mu^+_\beta + (1-\alpha)\mu^-_\beta$ of the plus and minus states, with $\alpha = (m^*_\beta + \mu(\sigma_0))/(2m^*_\beta)$. So every Gibbs measure is translation invariant, and $\mu^\pm_\beta$ are the only [extremal](c:extreme-point) ones.

hypotheses.text: The model is the nearest-neighbour ferromagnetic [Ising model](c:ising-model) on $\mathbb Z^2$ with zero field.
The [inverse temperature](c:inverse-temperature) satisfies $\beta > \beta_c$, so the [spontaneous magnetization](c:spontaneous-magnetization) $m^*_\beta$ is positive.
$\mu$ is an infinite-volume [Gibbs measure](c:gibbs-measure): it satisfies the DLR equations in every finite box.

proofs.name: Finite-volume proof by interface fluctuations
proofs.slogan: In a large box with any boundary condition, at most one interface comes near the centre, and its diffusive wandering makes it miss a small central box.
proofs.scope: The case $\beta > \beta_c$, as an outline of the proof of Coquille and Velenik. The contour estimates and the Ornstein-Zernike prefactors are cited from the source.

roles.why: Planar duality gives the random-line representation and the surface tension of the two-dimensional model.
For $\beta > \beta_c$ the surface tension is a norm with the sharp triangle inequality, and $m^*_\beta > 0$ fixes $\alpha$.
The DLR equations write $\mu$ as an average of finite-volume states over boundary conditions.

steps.slogan: Show that contours with far endpoints rarely reach the centre, by the sharp triangle inequality for [surface tension](c:norm).
steps.detail: A contour from $b$ to $b'$ that detours through a point at distance $n^a$ from the segment $bb'$ pays an extra surface cost of order $n^{2a-1}$. FKG and a union bound over endpoint pairs give probability at most $e^{-C n^{2a-1}}$.

steps.slogan: Show that at most one open contour crosses the central box $\Lambda_{n^a}$.
steps.detail: Two neighbouring crossing contours have nearby endpoints on both sides, so together they cost about $e^{-Cn}$ more than the boundary condition allows. The BK-type inequality for contour weights makes this precise.

steps.slogan: Bound the probability that the unique interface hits the small box $\Lambda_{2n^\xi}$ by $C n^{\xi - a/2}$.
steps.detail: Ornstein-Zernike prefactors $n^{-a/2}$ for the partition function and $n^{-a}$ for contours through a point give this bound after a sum over $O(n^\xi)$ points. The interface fluctuates on the scale $n^{a/2}$, which is much larger than $n^\xi$.

steps.slogan: Find a circuit of constant spin around the centre and compare with the [plus and minus states](c:boundary-condition).
steps.detail: Inside the largest constant-spin circuit the state has a constant boundary condition. Exponential relaxation in the pure phases gives $\langle f\rangle^\omega_{\Lambda_n} = \alpha_{n,\omega}\langle f\rangle^+_\beta + (1-\alpha_{n,\omega})\langle f\rangle^-_\beta + O(\|f\|_\infty n^{-\delta})$.

steps.slogan: Average the finite-volume estimate over the boundary condition with the DLR equations to identify $\mu$.
steps.detail: Integrating against $\mu$ gives $\mu(f) = A_n\langle f\rangle^+_\beta + (1-A_n)\langle f\rangle^-_\beta + O(n^{-\delta})$. The case $f = \sigma_0$ and $m^*_\beta > 0$ give $A_n \to \alpha$, and the limit gives $\mu = \alpha\mu^+_\beta + (1-\alpha)\mu^-_\beta$.

concepts.c:ising-model: The theorem classifies the Gibbs measures of the two-dimensional Ising model.
concepts.c:gibbs-measure: The DLR equations define the measures that the theorem classifies.
concepts.c:extreme-point: The plus and minus states are the extreme points of the segment of Gibbs measures.
concepts.c:inverse-temperature: The proof works in the low-temperature region $\beta > \beta_c$.
concepts.c:spontaneous-magnetization: Positive spontaneous magnetization lets $\mu(\sigma_0)$ determine the weight $\alpha$.
concepts.c:norm: The surface tension is a norm, and its sharp triangle inequality penalizes detours of contours.

new_concepts.name: Gibbs measure
new_concepts.reminder: A Gibbs measure is an infinite-volume law whose conditional law in each finite box is the finite Gibbs distribution.
new_concepts.definition: For finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$ and a [boundary condition](c:boundary-condition) $\eta$, let $\pi_\Lambda^\eta$ be the finite-volume [Gibbs distribution](c:gibbs-distribution) of an interaction in $\Lambda$, with the spins outside $\Lambda$ fixed to $\eta$. A [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu$ on the configuration space $S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ is a Gibbs measure if, for every finite $\Lambda$, the [conditional distribution](c:conditional-distribution) of the spins in $\Lambda$ given the spins outside $\Lambda$ is $\pi_\Lambda^\eta$ for $\mu$-almost every outside configuration $\eta$. new_concepts.name: inverse temperature
new_concepts.reminder: The inverse temperature $\beta=1/(k_BT)$ multiplies the energy in the Boltzmann weight $e^{-\beta H}$.
new_concepts.definition: The inverse temperature of a system at absolute temperature $T$ is $\beta=1/(k_BT)$, where $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant. It is the parameter in the [Boltzmann distribution](c:boltzmann-distribution) $\mu_\beta(\sigma)=e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}/Z(\beta)$ of a [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) $H$. new_concepts.name: spontaneous magnetization
new_concepts.reminder: The spontaneous magnetization $m^*(\beta)=\lim_{h\downarrow0}\langle\sigma_0\rangle_{\beta,h}$ is the magnetization that remains when the external field vanishes.
new_concepts.definition: For the [Ising model](c:ising-model) on $\mathbb Z^d$ at [inverse temperature](c:inverse-temperature) $\beta$, the spontaneous magnetization is $m^*(\beta)=\lim_{h\downarrow0}\langle\sigma_0\rangle_{\beta,h}$, where $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\beta,h}$ is the infinite-volume state in the field $h>0$. statement: For the ferromagnetic [Ising model](c:ising-model) on the $(k+1)$-regular [tree](c:tree) with $k \ge 2$, the root magnetization under the plus [boundary condition](c:boundary-condition) has a positive limit if and only if $k \tanh \beta > 1$. So the [critical temperature](c:critical-temperature) is given by $\beta_c = \operatorname{atanh}(1/k)$.

hypotheses.text: The graph is the $(k+1)$-regular [tree](c:tree) with $k \ge 2$ and root $o$.
The [Ising model](c:ising-model) has coupling $1$ on every edge, [inverse temperature](c:inverse-temperature) $\beta \ge 0$ and zero field.

conclusion: $|\mu^\eta_{n,\beta}(\sigma_o)| \le m_n(\beta) \downarrow m(\beta)$ for every boundary condition $\eta$, and the [spontaneous magnetization](c:spontaneous-magnetization) $m(\beta)$ is positive if and only if $\beta > \operatorname{atanh}(1/k) = \tfrac12 \ln\frac{k+1}{k-1}$.

proofs.name: Cavity recursion
proofs.slogan: Propagate effective fields from the boundary to the root with $f(h) = \operatorname{atanh}(\tanh\beta \tanh h)$ and study the fixed points of $kf$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for the root magnetization in finite volume and its limit. It does not treat all infinite-volume Gibbs measures.

roles.why: In a tree the subtrees of the children are disjoint, so partition functions factorize, and regularity makes all plus fields at one height equal.
A ferromagnetic coupling makes $f$ odd, increasing and concave on $[0,\infty)$, with $f'(0) = \tanh\beta$.

steps.slogan: Write the field of each vertex as the sum of $f$ over the fields of its children.
steps.detail: The partition function of a subtree factorizes over the children, and $\sum_t e^{\beta s t + h t} = 2\cosh(\beta s + h)$. This gives $h_x = \sum_y f(h_y)$ with $f(h) = \operatorname{atanh}(\tanh\beta\tanh h)$, $f(\pm\infty) = \pm\beta$, and root magnetization $\tanh(\sum_{y} f(h_y))$ over the $k+1$ children of $o$, a formula with the [hyperbolic tangent](c:hyperbolic-function).

steps.slogan: Show that the plus-boundary fields decrease to the largest [fixed point](c:fixed-point) of $kf$.
steps.detail: The plus fields satisfy $a_0 = \infty$ and $a_{j+1} = k f(a_j)$. Since $kf$ is increasing and $a_1 \le a_0$, the sequence decreases to $a^* \ge 0$, and every nonnegative fixed point lies below every $a_j$. So $m_n = \tanh((k+1)f(a_{n-1}))$ decreases to $\tanh((k+1)f(a^*))$.

steps.slogan: Decide by [concavity](c:concave-function) whether $kf$ has a positive fixed point.
steps.detail: The function $\psi = kf - \mathrm{id}$ is strictly concave on $[0,\infty)$ with $\psi(0) = 0$ and $\psi'(0) = k\tanh\beta - 1$. If this slope is at most $0$, then $\psi < 0$ on $(0,\infty)$. If it is positive, $\psi$ changes sign before $k\beta$ and the intermediate value theorem gives a positive fixed point.

steps.slogan: Bound the field for every [boundary condition](c:boundary-condition) by the plus field at the same height.
steps.detail: Induction on the height with $|f(h)| = f(|h|)$ gives $|h_x| \le a_j$ for every boundary condition, so $|\mu^\eta_{n,\beta}(\sigma_o)| \le m_n$. Spin-flip symmetry gives $-m_n$ for the minus boundary, and the fixed-point dichotomy gives $\beta_c = \operatorname{atanh}(1/k)$.

new_concepts.name: critical temperature
new_concepts.reminder: The critical temperature $T_c=1/(k_B\beta_c)$ separates the disordered phase at high temperature from the ordered phase at low temperature.
new_concepts.definition: The critical temperature $T_c$ of a spin model is the temperature at which the model passes from a disordered phase, with a unique [Gibbs measure](c:gibbs-measure), to an ordered phase. For the [Ising model](c:ising-model) at $h=0$, the critical inverse temperature is $\beta_c=\inf\{\beta\ge0:m^*(\beta)>0\}$, where $m^*$ is the [spontaneous magnetization](c:spontaneous-magnetization), and $T_c=1/(k_B\beta_c)$.

new_concepts.name: free energy
new_concepts.reminder: The free energy is $-1/\beta$ times the pressure $\psi=\lim|\Lambda|^{-1}\log Z_\Lambda$ of a lattice model.
new_concepts.definition: For a lattice spin model with [partition function](c:partition-function) $Z_\Lambda(\beta)$ in a finite box $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$, the pressure is the [thermodynamic limit](c:thermodynamic-limit) $\psi(\beta)=\lim_{\Lambda\uparrow\mathbb Z^d}|\Lambda|^{-1}\log Z_\Lambda(\beta)$. The free energy per site is $f(\beta)=-\psi(\beta)/\beta$, where $\beta$ is the [inverse temperature](c:inverse-temperature). For finite-range interactions, the limit exists along boxes, it does not depend on the boundary condition, and $\psi$ is convex.

statement: In the [Curie-Weiss model](c:curie-weiss-model) with $N$ spins at [inverse temperature](c:inverse-temperature) $\beta$, the magnetization $m_N$ concentrates at $0$ when $\beta \le 1$. When $\beta > 1$ it concentrates at $\pm m^*(\beta)$, where $m^*$ is the positive solution of $\tanh(\beta m) = m$, and each sign has limit probability $1/2$. This is a [phase transition](c:phase-transition) at $\beta_c = 1$.

hypotheses.text: The spins $\sigma \in \{-1,1\}^N$ have the [Curie-Weiss](c:curie-weiss-model) law $\mu_{N,\beta}(\sigma) \propto \exp(\beta M_N^2/(2N))$ with $M_N = \sum_i \sigma_i$.
The [inverse temperature](c:inverse-temperature) $\beta \ge 0$ is fixed while $N \to \infty$.

conclusion: For $\beta \le 1$, $\mu_{N,\beta}(|m_N| \ge \varepsilon) \le e^{-cN}$. For $\beta > 1$, $\mu_{N,\beta}(||m_N| - m^*| \ge \varepsilon) \le e^{-cN}$ and $\mu_{N,\beta}(|m_N \mp m^*| < \varepsilon) \to 1/2$, with [spontaneous magnetization](c:spontaneous-magnetization) $m^* > 0$.

proofs.name: Free energy of the magnetization
proofs.slogan: Count configurations by their magnetization, compare the counts with an entropy, and locate the maximizers of the resulting free energy.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every $\beta \ge 0$. The proof gives exponential bounds with a constant $c$ that it does not compute.

roles.why: The weight depends on $\sigma$ only through $m_N$, so the law of $m_N$ is a [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient) times an explicit factor.
The value of $\beta$ against $1$ decides whether $0$ or $\pm m^*$ maximizes the free energy.

steps.slogan: Write the law of the magnetization with a [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient).
steps.detail: Exactly $\binom{N}{k}$ configurations have $k$ plus spins and $m_N = (2k-N)/N$. So $\mu_{N,\beta}(m_N = m) = Z^{-1}\binom{N}{k} e^{\beta N m^2/2}$ on the grid $A_N = \{-1 + 2k/N\}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the binomial coefficient above and below by the exponential of the [entropy](c:entropy).
steps.detail: The binomial$(N, k/N)$ probabilities sum to $1$ and are largest at $k$. Hence $(N+1)^{-1}e^{N s(m)} \le \binom{N}{k} \le e^{N s(m)}$, where $s(m)$ is the binary entropy of $(1+m)/2$.

steps.slogan: Show that sets away from the maximizers of $\varphi$ have exponentially small probability.
steps.detail: With $\varphi(m) = \beta m^2/2 + s(m)$, the two bounds give $\mu(m_N \in F) \le (N+1)^2 e^{-N(\max\varphi - \sup_F \varphi - \delta_N)}$. Uniform continuity of $\varphi$ and the mesh $2/N$ of the grid give $\delta_N \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Locate the maximizers of $\varphi$ through the mean-field equation $\tanh(\beta m) = m$.
steps.detail: Since $\varphi'(m) = m(\beta - g(m))$ with $g(m) = \operatorname{atanh}(m)/m$ strictly increasing from $1$ to $\infty$, the only maximizer is $0$ if $\beta \le 1$. If $\beta > 1$, the maximizers are exactly $\pm m^*$ with $g(m^*) = \beta$, which is the equation $\tanh(\beta m^*) = m^*$ for the [hyperbolic tangent](c:hyperbolic-function).

steps.slogan: Split the probability equally between the two signs with the spin-flip symmetry.
steps.detail: The compact set of points at distance at least $\varepsilon$ from the maximizers has a strictly smaller maximum of $\varphi$, so its probability is at most $e^{-cN}$. The map $\sigma \mapsto -\sigma$ preserves the law, so the neighbourhoods of $m^*$ and $-m^*$ each get probability tending to $1/2$.

statement: In the [Curie-Weiss model](c:curie-weiss-model), the total spin $S_N$ satisfies $S_N/\sqrt N \Rightarrow N(0, 1/(1-\beta))$ for $\beta < 1$, $S_N/N^{3/4} \Rightarrow$ the law with density proportional to $e^{-x^4/12}$ at the [critical temperature](c:critical-temperature) $\beta = 1$, and $S_N/N \Rightarrow \frac12(\delta_{m^*} + \delta_{-m^*})$ for $\beta > 1$.

hypotheses.text: For each $N$ the spins have the [Curie-Weiss](c:curie-weiss-model) law proportional to $\exp(\beta S_N^2/(2N))$ on $\{-1,1\}^N$.
The [inverse temperature](c:inverse-temperature) $\beta \ge 0$ is fixed as $N \to \infty$.

conclusion: Each rescaled total spin converges in distribution ([convergence in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution)): to a [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution) for $\beta < 1$, to the density $\propto e^{-x^4/12}$ for $\beta = 1$, and to two atoms at $\pm m^*$ for $\beta > 1$.

proofs.name: Gaussian transform and Laplace limit
proofs.slogan: Add an independent Gaussian to linearize the quadratic weight, find an explicit density, and pass to the limit in its exponent.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Part (c) is taken from the Curie-Weiss phase transition theorem, and $\beta = 0$ from the classical central limit theorem.

roles.why: The weight depends only on $S_N^2$, so a Gaussian shift turns it into a product of $\cosh$ factors.
The value of $\beta$ fixes the scaling exponent and the leading term of $G$ near its minimum.

steps.slogan: Write the law of a Gaussian-smoothed total spin as an explicit [density](c:probability-density-function).
steps.detail: With $W \sim N(0, 1/\beta)$ independent, $Y_N = W/N^{1/2-\gamma} + S_N/N^{1-\gamma}$ has density proportional to $\exp(-N G(y/N^\gamma))$ with $G(u) = \beta u^2/2 - \log\cosh(\beta u)$. The square $S_N^2$ cancels and the sum over spins factorizes into $\cosh$ terms.

steps.slogan: Remove the Gaussian smoothing with [characteristic functions](c:characteristic-function) when $\beta < 1$.
steps.detail: For $\gamma = 1/2$ the exponent $N G(y/\sqrt N)$ tends to $\beta(1-\beta)y^2/2$ and stays above it, so dominated convergence gives the limit of $Y_N$. Dividing the characteristic function by $e^{-t^2/(2\beta)}$ and using Lévy's continuity theorem gives $N(0, 1/(1-\beta))$ for $S_N/\sqrt N$.

steps.slogan: Expand $G$ to fourth order at $\beta = 1$ and pass to the quartic limit.
steps.detail: For $\gamma = 1/4$ the quadratic terms of $G$ cancel and $N G(y/N^{1/4}) \to y^4/12$. The bounds $G(u) \ge \tanh^2(1)u^4/12$ for $|u| \le 1$ and $G(u) \ge G(1)|u|$ beyond give domination, and Slutsky's theorem removes $W/N^{1/4}$.

steps.slogan: Read the two-atom limit for $\beta > 1$ from the phase transition theorem.
steps.detail: The phase transition theorem puts $S_N/N$ within $\varepsilon$ of $m^*$ or of $-m^*$ with probability $1/2$ each in the limit, which is convergence to $\frac12(\delta_{m^*} + \delta_{-m^*})$.

steps.slogan: Collect the three regimes into the [convergence in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) statement.
steps.detail: The scales $\sqrt N$, $N^{3/4}$ and $N$ and the three limit laws come from the previous steps. Their change at $\beta = 1$ marks the critical point of the model.

concepts.c:probability-density-function: The Gaussian transform gives an explicit density for the smoothed total spin.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: Characteristic functions remove the independent Gaussian smoothing.

new_concepts.name: Gibbs measure
new_concepts.reminder: A Gibbs measure is an infinite-volume law whose conditional law in each finite box is the finite Gibbs distribution.
new_concepts.definition: For finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$ and a [boundary condition](c:boundary-condition) $\eta$, let $\pi_\Lambda^\eta$ be the finite-volume [Gibbs distribution](c:gibbs-distribution) of an interaction in $\Lambda$, with the spins outside $\Lambda$ fixed to $\eta$. A [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu$ on the configuration space $S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ is a Gibbs measure if, for every finite $\Lambda$, the [conditional distribution](c:conditional-distribution) of the spins in $\Lambda$ given the spins outside $\Lambda$ is $\pi_\Lambda^\eta$ for $\mu$-almost every outside configuration $\eta$. These conditions are the DLR equations.

new_concepts.name: inverse temperature
new_concepts.reminder: The inverse temperature $\beta=1/(k_BT)$ multiplies the energy in the Boltzmann weight $e^{-\beta H}$.
new_concepts.definition: The inverse temperature of a system at absolute temperature $T$ is $\beta=1/(k_BT)$, where $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant. It is the parameter in the [Boltzmann distribution](c:boltzmann-distribution) $\mu_\beta(\sigma)=e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}/Z(\beta)$ of a [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) $H$. Mathematical texts usually set $k_B=1$ and use $\beta\in[0,\infty)$ as the parameter.

new_concepts.name: phase transition
new_concepts.reminder: A phase transition is a parameter value where the infinite-volume free energy is not analytic or several Gibbs measures coexist.
new_concepts.definition: A phase transition of a lattice model is a value of its parameters, such as the inverse temperature $\beta$ and the field $h$, at which the infinite-volume [free energy](c:free-energy) is not real-analytic. It is first-order when a first derivative of the free energy is discontinuous there. In the [Ising model](c:ising-model) this happens at $h=0$ and $\beta>\beta_c$, where the derivative in $h$ jumps and several infinite-volume [Gibbs measures](c:gibbs-measure) coexist.

new_concepts.name: spontaneous magnetization
new_concepts.reminder: The spontaneous magnetization $m^*(\beta)=\lim_{h\downarrow0}\langle\sigma_0\rangle_{\beta,h}$ is the magnetization that remains when the external field vanishes.
new_concepts.definition: For the [Ising model](c:ising-model) on $\mathbb Z^d$ at [inverse temperature](c:inverse-temperature) $\beta$, the spontaneous magnetization is $m^*(\beta)=\lim_{h\downarrow0}\langle\sigma_0\rangle_{\beta,h}$, where $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\beta,h}$ is the infinite-volume state in the field $h>0$. It equals $\langle\sigma_0\rangle^+_\beta$, the [expected value](c:expected-value) of the spin at the origin under the plus Gibbs measure at $h=0$, and also the right derivative $\partial\psi/\partial h(\beta,0^+)$ of the pressure. For $d\ge2$, $m^*(\beta)=0$ for $\beta\le\beta_c$ and $m^*(\beta)>0$ for $\beta>\beta_c$.

statement: For every locally finite, infinite [rooted tree](c:rooted-tree) $T$, the [critical probability](c:critical-probability) of Bernoulli bond [percolation](c:percolation) is $p_c(T) = 1/\operatorname{br} T$, where $\operatorname{br} T$ is the [branching number](c:branching-number).

hypotheses.text: $T$ is an infinite [tree](c:tree) with root $o$ in which every vertex has finite degree.
Each edge is open with probability $p$, independently of the others.

conclusion: $\mathbb{P}_p(o \leftrightarrow \infty) = 0$ for $p < 1/\operatorname{br} T$ and $\mathbb{P}_p(o \leftrightarrow \infty) > 0$ for $p > 1/\operatorname{br} T$, so $p_c(T) = 1/\operatorname{br} T$.

proofs.name: First and second moments along flows
proofs.slogan: A small cutset sum kills percolation by a first-moment bound, and a flow below $\lambda^{-|x|}$ gives a bounded second moment that forces percolation.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with the explicit bound $\mathbb{P}_p(o \leftrightarrow \infty) \ge s(p\lambda - 1)/(s(p\lambda-1) + 1 - p)$. The critical case $p = 1/\operatorname{br} T$ is not covered.

roles.why: Paths in a tree are unique, so $\mathbb{P}_p(o \leftrightarrow x) = p^{|x|}$, and local finiteness gives Kőnig's lemma and finite levels.
Independence gives the exact probabilities $p^{|x|}$ and $p^{2n - |x \wedge y|}$ for open paths.

steps.slogan: Turn a positive infimum of cutset sums into an admissible [flow](c:flow-network) by finite max-flow min-cut.
steps.detail: If $\inf_\Pi \sum_{x \in \Pi} p^{|x|} = \delta > 0$, max-flow min-cut on the ball of radius $n$ gives flows of strength $\delta$ with $\theta_n(x) \le p^{|x|}$. A diagonal subsequence converges at every vertex to a flow on $T$, so $\operatorname{br} T \ge 1/p$.

steps.slogan: Bound the percolation probability by a cutset sum when $p < 1/\operatorname{br} T$.
steps.detail: An infinite cluster contains an open ray from $o$ by Kőnig's lemma, and the ray crosses every cutset $\Pi$. The union bound gives $\mathbb{P}_p(o \leftrightarrow \infty) \le \sum_{x \in \Pi} p^{|x|}$, and the previous step makes the infimum of the right side zero.

steps.slogan: Bound the second moment of the flow-weighted count of open level-$n$ vertices.
steps.detail: For $1/p < \lambda < \operatorname{br} T$ take a flow of strength $s$ below $\lambda^{-|x|}$ and $X_n = \sum_{|x| = n} \theta(x) p^{-n} \mathbf{1}[o \leftrightarrow x]$. Then the [expected value](c:expected-value) of $X_n$ is $s$ and $\mathbb{E}X_n^2 = s^2 + (1-p)\sum_{1 \le |u| \le n} p^{-|u|}\theta(u)^2 \le s^2 + (1-p)s/(p\lambda - 1)$.

steps.slogan: Pass the second-moment lower bound to the limit and identify the [critical probability](c:critical-probability).
steps.detail: Cauchy-Schwarz gives $\mathbb{P}(X_n > 0) \ge (\mathbb{E}X_n)^2/\mathbb{E}X_n^2$, which is bounded below uniformly in $n$. The events that $o$ reaches level $n$ decrease to $\{o \leftrightarrow \infty\}$, so this probability is positive for $p > 1/\operatorname{br} T$.

concepts.c:rooted-tree: The theorem concerns percolation from the root of a fixed tree.
concepts.c:critical-probability: The critical probability is the quantity that the theorem computes.
concepts.c:percolation: Bernoulli bond percolation is the random model on the tree.
concepts.c:branching-number: The branching number is the flow capacity that equals $1/p_c$.
concepts.c:tree: Unique paths in a tree give exact connection probabilities.
concepts.c:flow-network: Flows bounded by $\lambda^{-|x|}$ define the branching number and weight the second moment.
concepts.c:expected-value: The first moment of $X_n$ equals the strength of the flow.

source.ref: R. Lyons and Y. Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks (CUP 2016), Theorem 5.15, p. 145, with the bound (5.6), p. 140, and Theorem 5.14, p. 144.

new_concepts.name: branching number
new_concepts.reminder: The branching number of a tree measures its average number of branches per vertex through flows.
new_concepts.definition: For a locally finite [rooted tree](c:rooted-tree) $T$, the branching number $\operatorname{br} T$ is the supremum of the $\lambda > 0$ for which some nonzero [flow](c:flow-network) from the root satisfies $\theta(x) \le \lambda^{-|x|}$ at every vertex $x$.

new_concepts.name: critical probability
new_concepts.reminder: The critical probability $p_c$ is the threshold above which Bernoulli percolation has an infinite open cluster.
new_concepts.definition: For [Bernoulli percolation](c:percolation) on an infinite connected graph $G$, let $\theta(p)$ be the probability that a fixed vertex lies in an infinite open cluster. The critical probability is $p_c(G)=\sup\{p\in[0,1]:\theta(p)=0\}$. By the Kolmogorov zero-one law, an infinite open cluster exists with probability $0$ when $p<p_c$ and with probability $1$ when $p>p_c$.

new_concepts.name: Bernoulli percolation
new_concepts.reminder: Bernoulli percolation keeps each edge of a graph independently with probability $p$ and studies the connected clusters.
new_concepts.definition: Bernoulli bond percolation with parameter $p\in[0,1]$ on a [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$ declares each edge open with probability $p$ and closed otherwise, independently of all other edges. Its law is the [product measure](c:product-measure) $\mathbb P_p=\bigotimes_{e\in E}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ on $\{0,1\}^E$. The open clusters are the [connected components](c:connected-component) of the graph $(V,\{e:\omega(e)=1\})$, and site percolation does the same with vertices.
